answer_text:
Let

\[
\mathcal M=\{f:\mathbb Q\to \mathbb Q \mid f \text{ is monotonic}\}.
\]

Interpreting “monotonic” in the usual non-strict sense (nondecreasing or nonincreasing), the cardinality is the cardinality of the continuum.

---

### 1. Upper bound

Since \(\mathbb Q\) is countably infinite, the set of all functions \(\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q\) has cardinality

\[
|\mathbb Q|^{|\mathbb Q|}=\aleph_0^{\aleph_0}.
\]

But

\[
2^{\aleph_0}\le \aleph_0^{\aleph_0}\le (2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}
=2^{\aleph_0\cdot \aleph_0}
=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

Thus

\[
|\mathbb Q^{\mathbb Q}|=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

Since \(\mathcal M\subseteq \mathbb Q^{\mathbb Q}\),

\[
|\mathcal M|\le 2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

---

### 2. Lower bound

For each real number \(x\in\mathbb R\), define \(f_x:\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q\) by

\[
f_x(q)=
\begin{cases}
0, & q<x,\\
1, & q\ge x.
\end{cases}
\]

Each \(f_x\) is nondecreasing, and its values lie in \(\{0,1\}\subseteq\mathbb Q\).

Now suppose \(x<y\). By density of \(\mathbb Q\) in \(\mathbb R\), there is some \(q\in\mathbb Q\) with

\[
x<q<y.
\]

Then

\[
f_x(q)=1 \qquad\text{but}\qquad f_y(q)=0,
\]

so \(f_x\neq f_y\). Hence the map

\[
x\longmapsto f_x
\]

is injective from \(\mathbb R\) into \(\mathcal M\). Therefore

\[
|\mathcal M|\ge |\mathbb R|=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

---

Combining the upper and lower bounds gives

\[
|\mathcal M|=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]

Equivalently, the cardinality is the continuum \(\mathfrak c\).

\[
\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}
\]

---

### Remark on strict monotonicity

If “monotonic” is intended to mean **strictly** monotonic, the answer is still \(2^{\aleph_0}\). The upper bound is unchanged. For a lower bound, one can encode arbitrary binary sequences into strictly increasing functions \(\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q\). For example, for each \(b=(b_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}\), define

\[
s_n=n+\frac{b_n}{2^{|n|+1}},
\]

and then define

\[
f_b(q)=q+s_{\lfloor q\rfloor}.
\]

The sequence \((s_n)\) is strictly increasing, and \(f_b\) is strictly increasing from \(\mathbb Q\) to \(\mathbb Q\). Different binary sequences give different functions, giving \(2^{\aleph_0}\) such functions. Thus the cardinality remains

\[
\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}.
\]
